description: The syllabus, a full glossary and four cheat sheets. Reference material, readable at any point.

lessons.title: Syllabus
lessons.description: The whole course in one place: modules, the 8-week plan, assessment and what you need.
lessons.content:
Everything about how this course is structured, assessed and paced, in one place.

## What this course is

A practical introduction to generative AI for people who have never studied it. Roughly **30 per cent concepts and 70 per cent hands-on**: most of your time is spent with the tools open, writing prompts, comparing outputs, generating images, and building something in Python.

It assumes no programming background. The modules that involve code introduce Python gently and give you starter code, hints and a full worked solution for every exercise.

**Who it is for:** college students, MBA students, freshers, non-technical professionals, and technical learners who want a practical start.

## The shape of it

**14 teaching modules, plus this reference section. 163 lessons. About 72 hours.**

Every teaching lesson follows the same four beats:

- **Learn** -- the concept, in plain English
- **Demonstrate** -- one worked, concrete example
- **Practice** -- something you do before moving on
- **What to remember** -- four or five bullets

Every module ends with the same three things: **practice questions with a full answer key**, a **hands-on lab**, and an **assignment marked against a published rubric**.

## The modules

**Level 1 -- GenAI Fundamentals**

1. **Introduction to AI and Generative AI** -- what AI is, how generative AI differs, where it genuinely helps and fails
2. **How Generative AI Works** *(code)* -- neural networks, LLMs, tokens, context, embeddings, transformers
3. **Understanding LLMs** -- the model families, open versus proprietary, choosing one, hallucination in depth
4. **Prompt Engineering** *(code)* -- the highest-leverage skill in the course
5. **Generative AI Tools** -- ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Claude, Perplexity, NotebookLM, GitHub Copilot
   -- ends with the **Level 1 exam**

**Level 2 -- GenAI Practitioner**

6. **AI for Productivity** -- study, research, presentations, spreadsheets, documents, email, meetings
7. **Generative AI for Images** -- how it works, prompting, style vocabulary, editing, posters
8. **Generative AI for Video and Audio** -- video, avatars, voice, music, scripts, editing
9. **Generative AI for Coding** *(code)* -- generating, explaining, debugging, documenting
10. **Responsible and Ethical AI** -- bias, privacy, copyright, deepfakes, misinformation, security
11. **Introduction to AI Agents** *(code)* -- tools, function calling, memory, planning, safety
12. **Building a Simple GenAI Application** *(code)* -- from an API call to a deployed app
13. **RAG: Introduction** *(code)* -- retrieval-augmented generation, end to end
    -- ends with the **Level 2 exam**

**Level 3 -- GenAI Project**

14. **Final Capstone Project** *(code)* -- plan, build and present a working application

**15. Course reference** -- this syllabus, the glossary and the cheat sheets

## The 8-week plan

A comfortable pace at a few hours a week. The course is self-paced, so go faster or slower.

- **Week 1** -- AI and generative AI fundamentals *(module 1)*
- **Week 2** -- LLMs and how GenAI works *(modules 2 and 3)*
- **Week 3** -- Prompt engineering *(module 4)*
- **Week 4** -- The tools and AI for productivity *(modules 5 and 6, then the Level 1 exam)*
- **Week 5** -- Image, video and audio generation *(modules 7 and 8)*
- **Week 6** -- AI coding and AI agents *(modules 9, 10 and 11)*
- **Week 7** -- Building applications and RAG *(modules 12 and 13, then the Level 2 exam)*
- **Week 8** -- Capstone project and presentation *(module 14)*

## How you are assessed

Four kinds of work, and only two of them are graded.

**Practice questions** close every module. Ungraded, self-marked, with a full explanation for every option. They are for you.

**Labs** are guided, hands-on, and produce something you can look at. Not separately graded; the work feeds the assignment.

**Assignments** close every module and are marked out of 100 against a rubric published in the lesson. You always know what you are being marked on before you start.

**Two exams and a capstone** award the certification levels:

- **Level 1 -- GenAI Fundamentals.** Twenty questions plus two applied tasks, at the end of module 5. Pass: 28 of 40.
- **Level 2 -- GenAI Practitioner.** Twenty questions plus two applied tasks, at the end of module 13. Pass: 28 of 40.
- **Level 3 -- GenAI Project.** The module 14 capstone: a working application, an evaluation, and a ten-minute presentation.

These are completion certificates from this platform recording what you finished here. **They are not vendor certifications** from OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or Anthropic.

## What you need

**A computer with a browser and a stable connection.**

**Free accounts on a few AI tools.** The lessons walk you through it. Every tool used has offered a free tier, but features and limits change often -- check what each currently offers rather than trusting any course.

**Python**, for modules 2, 4, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 14. Installed when you reach module 2. No prior experience needed.

**An API key** for module 12 onwards. Providers offer small free allowances or low-cost usage. Set a spending limit on your account before your first call.

## The rules this course works by

**Verify what you will be held to.** Every factual claim a model produces needs checking before you rely on it. This is not a formality; it is the single habit that separates useful work from embarrassing work.

**Know your institution's policy.** Rules on AI-assisted work vary widely and are enforced. Find out before you submit anything.

**Say when you used AI.** Several assignments ask for this explicitly. It costs nothing and it is increasingly expected.

**Nothing here is stated as a fixed fact if it will go stale.** You will not find prices, model version numbers, context window sizes or feature lists asserted as current, because they would be wrong within months. Where a lesson names a tool, it tells you to check its current features yourself.

## How to use this course well

**Do the practice sections.** They are short and they are where the learning is. Reading a good explanation feels like understanding and is not.

**Struggle for ten minutes before asking.** Productive difficulty is not a bug in your study process.

**Write your own explanation from memory, then ask what you got wrong.** The single most valuable study loop in the course, and almost nobody does it.

**Keep what you build.** The prompt library from module 4, the cheat sheets here, the application from module 12. Several are things you will still be using in a year.

lessons.title: Glossary
lessons.description: Every term the course introduces, alphabetical, with the module that defines it.
lessons.content:
Every term the course introduces, with the module that defines it. Written to be read in any order and returned to.

## A

**Agent** *(module 11)* -- A model in a loop, with tools, working toward a goal. It chooses its own sequence of actions rather than following steps you wrote.

**Alignment** *(module 2)* -- The training stage, often using human feedback, that shapes which responses a model prefers: more helpful, less harmful, more willing to say it does not know.

**API** *(module 12)* -- Application programming interface. How one program talks to another. You send a request to a URL with some data, and get a response back.

**API key** *(module 12)* -- A string proving a request comes from your account. Anyone holding it can spend your money. Treat it exactly like a password.

**Approximate nearest neighbour** *(module 13)* -- How a vector database finds similar vectors quickly, occasionally missing one it should have found. Almost always worth the trade.

**Attention** *(module 2)* -- The mechanism that works out, for every piece of text, which other parts of the passage are relevant to it. What made transformers work.

## B

**Backpropagation** *(module 2)* -- The process that adjusts a network's weights during training, nudging each one in the direction that would have made the answer better.

**Bias** *(module 10)* -- Unwanted patterns learned from training material and reproduced in output. No intent is required for output to be unfair.

**Blast radius** *(module 11)* -- What an agent's tools can reach. A chatbot's is zero; an agent that can send email can send the wrong email.

## C

**Chain of thought** *(module 4)* -- Getting a model to write out its steps before answering, so each step conditions the next. Helps on multi-step reasoning, hurts on simple tasks.

**Chunk** *(module 13)* -- A piece of a document, sized to be retrieved on its own. You retrieve chunks, not documents.

**Context window** *(module 2)* -- How much text a model can consider at once, measured in tokens. Everything competes for it: instructions, conversation, pasted documents and the response.

**Cosine similarity** *(module 2)* -- A measure of how close two embeddings are, from -1 to 1. In practice you care about ranking rather than the number.

## D

**Deep learning** *(module 1)* -- Machine learning using neural networks with many layers, needing large amounts of data and computing power. Behind most of what people now call AI.

**Deepfake** *(module 10)* -- Synthetic media depicting a real person doing or saying something they did not. Never create one without explicit, informed consent.

**Diffusion model** *(module 7)* -- How most image generation works: start from random noise and repeatedly remove a little of it, steered by your prompt.

## E

**Embedding** *(module 2)* -- Text turned into a list of numbers such that similar meanings land close together. The foundation of semantic search and RAG.

## F

**Few-shot prompting** *(module 4)* -- Including two to five worked examples in the prompt. Makes your pattern the obvious continuation, and succeeds where descriptions fail.

**Fine-tuning** *(module 2)* -- Training an existing model further on your own examples. Real cost and expertise, and routinely reached for too early.

**Foundation model** *(module 2)* -- One large model trained broadly, then adapted cheaply to many tasks by prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning.

**Function calling** *(module 11)* -- See **tool**. The model produces a structured request to call a function; your code decides whether to run it.

## H

**Hallucination** *(modules 1, 3, 10)* -- A model stating something false with the same confidence as everything true. Not a fixable bug: it is the normal mechanism producing an unwanted output.

## I

**Image-to-image** *(module 7)* -- Generating from a picture you supply rather than pure noise. You control the first frame, so only the change is uncertain.

**Indemnity** *(module 7)* -- A provider's commitment to defend you if generated output is legally challenged. Matters for commercial use.

**Inference** *(module 2)* -- Running a trained model to produce output. The weights are frozen; nothing is learned.

**Inpainting** *(module 7)* -- Masking part of an image and describing what should be there instead. The workhorse of image editing.

## K

**Knowledge cutoff** *(module 3)* -- The point in time up to which a model's training material was gathered. A model does not reliably know where its own cutoff is.

## L

**Large language model (LLM)** *(module 2)* -- A neural network trained to predict what text comes next. Everything else it does is that one ability applied.

## M

**Machine learning** *(module 1)* -- Software that works out a rule from examples rather than being given the rule.

**Multimodal** *(module 3)* -- Handling more than one kind of input or output, usually images alongside text. Excellent at meaning, unreliable at precision.

## N

**Negative prompt** *(module 7)* -- A separate field, in tools that have one, for what you do not want. Negation inside the main prompt is unreliable.

**Neural network** *(module 2)* -- A very large mathematical function: numbers in, numbers out, arithmetic in between. The weights are the learned part.

**Non-determinism** *(module 1)* -- The same question producing different answers. A feature for creative work, a problem for anything repeatable.

## O

**Open weights** *(module 3)* -- A model whose trained weights are published, so you can run it yourself. Usually called "open source", which is generally inaccurate: the training data and code are not published.

**Outpainting** *(module 7)* -- Extending an image beyond its original edges.

## P

**Parameters** *(module 2)* -- A model's learned weights. Roughly its capacity to hold patterns. A poor way to compare models across families.

**Pre-training** *(module 2)* -- The long, expensive first training stage: predict the next token across a vast body of text.

**Prompt** *(module 4)* -- Everything sent to the model: standing instructions, the conversation so far, pasted material and your question. Not just what you typed.

**Prompt injection** *(module 10)* -- Instructions hidden in content a model reads, which it then follows. Has no complete fix; design assuming it can happen.

**Prompt template** *(module 4)* -- A good prompt with the changing parts marked, so it can be reused, tested and improved once for every future use.

## R

**RAG** *(module 13)* -- Retrieval-augmented generation. Find the relevant material and put it in the prompt before asking. Converts recall into transformation.

**Rate limit** *(module 12)* -- A cap on how many requests you may make in a period. A transient failure worth retrying with backoff.

**Relevance floor** *(module 13)* -- A minimum similarity score below which retrieved chunks are discarded, so the system can say it does not know instead of answering from irrelevant material.

**Role prompting** *(module 4)* -- Telling the model who to be. Changes tone, vocabulary and perspective. Adds no knowledge and no reliability.

## S

**Scratchpad** *(module 11)* -- A file an agent writes findings to and reads back. The simplest useful memory, and it survives context overflow.

**Seed** *(module 7)* -- The fixed starting point for generation, where a tool allows setting it. Same seed and prompt, same image.

**Semantic search** *(module 2)* -- Finding text by meaning rather than by matching words, using embeddings.

**Structured output** *(module 4)* -- Asking for a machine-readable reply, usually JSON, so the next step can use it without a person in between.

**System prompt** *(module 4)* -- The standing instruction applying to a whole conversation. Followed more consistently than instructions buried in a message.

## T

**Text-to-image** *(module 7)* -- Generating a picture from a description.

**Token** *(module 2)* -- A chunk of text a model reads and writes. Roughly four characters in English. Cost, rate limits and context windows are all counted in tokens.

**Tokenization** *(module 2)* -- Splitting text into tokens. Explains why character-counting tasks are oddly hard for models.

**Tool** *(module 11)* -- A function a model can request. The model never runs it; your code decides whether to.

**Training** *(module 2)* -- Building a model by adjusting weights over an enormous amount of data. Happens once, before you ever use it.

**Transformer** *(module 2)* -- The design behind modern language models. Reads a whole passage at once and uses attention to decide what is relevant to what.

## U

**Upscaling** *(module 7)* -- Increasing an image's resolution by inventing plausible detail. The detail is generated, not recovered.

## V

**Vector database** *(module 13)* -- Stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones quickly. Below about ten thousand chunks, a list and a loop is the right answer.

**Voice cloning** *(module 8)* -- Building a synthetic voice from a sample. Never without the person's explicit, informed consent.

## Z

**Zero-shot prompting** *(module 4)* -- Asking without examples. Fine for common, well-defined tasks.

lessons.title: Cheat sheet: prompt engineering
lessons.description: The six parts, the patterns, the ten mistakes and the pre-send checklist.
lessons.content:
One page for module 4. Print it, or keep it open while you work.

## The six parts of a prompt

1. **Role** -- who the model should be. Optional. Sets tone, not knowledge.
2. **Task** -- what to do. The part everyone includes.
3. **Context** -- the material and background. **The part most often missing.**
4. **Constraints** -- length, tone, what to include and avoid, what to do when unsure.
5. **Format** -- the shape of the output. Say it, or you get whatever the default is.
6. **Examples** -- one to five worked cases. The most powerful and least used.

**Order:** put long context *before* the instruction.

## The one line to always include

> If you are not certain, say so. If the information is not in what I gave you, say that rather than filling the gap.

Put it in your standing instructions and stop thinking about it.

## Diagnosing bad output

- **Too long or short** -- no length constraint
- **Wrong tone** -- audience unspecified
- **Missing something** -- state the requirement explicitly
- **Made something up** -- supply the source, add the uncertainty line
- **Wrong shape** -- format unspecified
- **Misunderstood the task** -- your instruction is ambiguous; reread it as a stranger
- **Right but generic** -- not enough context about your situation

Change **one thing** per round.

## Patterns

**Zero-shot** -- no examples. Common, well-defined tasks.

**Few-shot** -- two to five realistic examples, including an awkward one. Use when the format is unusual, the tone is hard to describe, or the categories are yours.

**Role** -- `"Explain this to a first-year undergraduate"` beats `"You are an expert"`. Specify audience and behaviour, not expertise.

**Chain of thought** -- name the steps yourself rather than saying "think step by step". Helps on multi-step reasoning, hurts on short tasks.

**Structured output:**

```
Return ONLY a JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{ "field": string or null, "category": one of "a", "b", "c" }
If a field is not stated, use null. Do not infer.
```

## The ten common mistakes

1. Assuming context the model does not have
2. Asking several things at once
3. Leaving the format unspecified
4. Prohibitions where specifications would work
5. Relying on recall instead of supplying the source
6. Believing the confidence
7. Not saying what to do when the answer is unknown
8. Tuning on one example
9. Cargo-culting magic phrases
10. Long conversations where a fresh one would be better

## The pre-send checklist

- Have I supplied the material, or am I relying on recall?
- Have I said who this is for?
- Have I said how long, and in what shape?
- Have I said what to do if it does not know?
- Am I asking one thing or several?

## Evaluating a prompt

Ten real inputs. Criteria written **before** you look at any output. Pass or fail per criterion. A record of prompt version, date and score.

Criteria must be specific enough that two people would mark the same way. "Is it accurate?" cannot be marked. "Does every factual claim appear in the source?" can.

Measure **invention** separately. It is the most dangerous failure and the easiest to miss.

lessons.title: Cheat sheet: image and video prompting
lessons.description: The style, lighting, composition and camera vocabulary, plus what does not work.
lessons.content:
The vocabulary from module 7, in one place. These words do more for your results than any technique.

## Prompt order

```
[style], [subject with detail], [setting], [lighting], [composition], [colour]
```

Lead with style. It changes an image more than anything else.

## Style

**Photographic** -- film photograph, digital photograph, documentary photography, studio photograph, polaroid, black and white photograph

**Illustrative** -- watercolour, oil painting, gouache, ink line drawing, charcoal sketch, woodblock print, children's book illustration, technical illustration, flat vector illustration

**Rendered** -- 3D render, clay render, isometric illustration, low-poly, product visualisation

**Graphic** -- minimalist poster, art deco poster, screen print, risograph, infographic, blueprint

## Composition

**Shot** -- extreme close-up, close-up, medium shot, wide shot, establishing shot

**Angle** -- eye level, low angle *(imposing)*, high angle *(diminished)*, overhead, dutch angle *(unsettling)*

**Arrangement** -- centred, rule of thirds, symmetrical, negative space, tight crop

**Depth** -- shallow depth of field, deep focus, bokeh

## Lighting

The main driver of mood, and the thing most often left out.

**Direction** -- backlit, side lighting, front lit, rim lighting, top-down

**Quality** -- soft diffused, harsh direct, dappled, overcast

**Time** -- golden hour, blue hour, midday sun, moonlight, candlelight, neon

**Studio** -- three-point, single softbox, **high key** *(bright, minimal shadow)*, **low key** *(dark, dramatic)*

High key and low key shift emotional register more reliably than any mood word.

## Camera

**Lens** -- wide angle, 35mm *(natural)*, 85mm portrait *(flattering)*, macro, telephoto *(compressed)*

**Finish** -- 35mm film grain, high contrast, desaturated, muted palette, vivid saturated

## What does not work

- **Instructions.** Describe the image as if it exists; do not command.
- **Negation.** "No cars" often produces cars. Use a negative prompt field if the tool has one.
- **Spatial placement.** Unreliable. Sketch the layout and use image-to-image.
- **Adjectives of approval.** "Beautiful, stunning, 8k, masterpiece" do almost nothing.

## Known weak points

Hands. Readable text. Exact counts. Precise values in charts. All need exact structure a statistical process does not enforce.

## For posters

**Generate the artwork with no text. Add text in a design tool.**

Prompt for space: *"large areas of negative space across the top third"*, *"simple uncluttered composition"*, *"muted low contrast colours"*.

Consistency across a set comes mostly from **fonts, colours and layout**, not from prompts.

## For video

**Image-to-video beats text-to-video** -- you control the first frame, so only the motion is uncertain.

Describe only the motion, and add **"Nothing else moves."**

**Animates well** -- water, smoke, steam, cloud, fire, fabric, slow camera moves.

**Does not** -- people doing specific things, precise specified actions, long clips.

Expect a hit rate around one in four. Generate accordingly.

## Script timing

**130 to 150 words a minute.** A two-minute video is about 280 words. First drafts are routinely a third too long -- read aloud and time it.

lessons.title: Cheat sheet: code, APIs and RAG
lessons.description: Key handling, model calls, agent tools, the RAG pipeline and the deploy checklist.
lessons.content:
The patterns from modules 9, 11, 12 and 13, in one place.

## Never, ever

```python
api_key = "...the actual key..."   # NO
```

```python
import os
api_key = os.environ["SERVICE_API_KEY"]   # yes
```

`.gitignore` listing `.env` is written **before** `.env` exists. If a key is ever exposed, **revoke it** -- deleting the file does not remove it from git history.

Set a spending limit on your provider account before your first call.

## Briefing a code request

- Language **and version**
- The input, precisely, with a real example
- The output, precisely
- **The edge cases** -- empty, missing, duplicate, wrong type
- Constraints -- no external libraries, must not modify the input
- Style -- type hints, docstrings
- *"State any assumption you had to make in a comment."*
- *"Also write tests for: the normal case, empty input, and one malformed entry."*

Small functions with clear contracts. **Never ask for a whole program.**

## The three rules

1. **Read it** before accepting it
2. **Run it** -- code that looks right and fails is the normal case
3. **Understand it**, or do not ship it

## Debugging: what to include

1. The code
2. The **full** error, not a description of it
3. What you expected
4. What actually happened

Ask for **the cause before the fix**. After two or three failed attempts, reset -- fresh conversation, smallest failing example, or ask for logging rather than a fix.

## The best question about any code

> What could go wrong with this?

## Config that fails clearly

```python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

key = os.environ.get("MODEL_API_KEY", "").strip()
if not key:
    raise SystemExit("MODEL_API_KEY is not set. Copy .env.example to .env and add your key.")
```

An empty value is as missing as an absent one -- `MODEL_API_KEY=` is a common mistake.

## Calling a model

One wrapper, in one file. Return a result the caller can check rather than raising into the interface.

**Retry:** network, rate limit, server errors. Back off 1s, 2s, 4s. Do not sleep after the last attempt.

**Never retry:** auth failures, invalid requests, refusals. They fail identically every time.

**Always check why generation stopped.** Output truncated by the length limit looks complete until you read the end.

Cap input length. Someone will paste a novel.

## Prompt templates

```python
from string import Template

TEMPLATE = Template("Explain $topic to $audience in $words words.")
TEMPLATE.substitute(topic="tokens", audience="a beginner", words=200)
```

`string.Template`, because prompts contain braces. `substitute`, **not** `safe_substitute` -- a missing value should fail loudly, not send a prompt containing `$topic`.

## Agent tools

The model **never** executes anything. It produces a request; your code decides.

- Few, narrow, clearly distinguished tools
- Say in the description **when to use it and what it does not cover**
- Separate reading from doing
- Validate arguments as untrusted input
- **Return errors, never raise** -- an agent that reads an error can recover
- Confirm anything irreversible
- Always a step limit, and a repeat check

## RAG pipeline

```
Documents -> Chunks -> Embeddings -> Vector store -> LLM
```

**Diagnose failures in that order.** The fault is usually earlier than you think.

- **Extraction** -- garbled text. Read a page of your extracted output before anything else.
- **Chunking** -- prepend the document title and section to each chunk. Overlap 10-20 per cent.
- **Embedding** -- same model for chunks and queries, always. Store the model name and refuse a mismatch.
- **Retrieval** -- add a relevance floor, or the system answers everything.
- **Generation** -- *"Use only the sources above. Cite the source number. If the sources do not answer, say exactly: The provided sources do not answer this question."*

Under ~10,000 chunks, a list and a loop beats a database.

Keep vectors and metadata **in the same order**, or every citation silently points at the wrong text.

## What to measure

Not just how many it got right:

- **Retrieval accuracy** -- was the right chunk in the top k?
- **Citation accuracy** -- does the citation point at the passage the answer came from?
- **Refusal rate** -- on questions the documents cannot answer
- **False refusals** -- questions it should have answered

A system that answers everything confidently answers questions it has no basis for.

## Before you deploy

- Runs from a **clean checkout** in a fresh virtual environment
- `requirements.txt` complete
- `git grep -i "api_key\|secret\|sk-"` finds nothing
- `.env` not in the repository, and not in its history
- Every failure path returns a message, not a stack trace
- Secrets in the platform's secrets panel, never a deployed `.env`
- A note telling users what it is, what it is not, and that output needs checking

lessons.title: Cheat sheet: responsible use and verification
lessons.description: What to verify, what never to do, the four tests, and disclosure.
lessons.content:
Module 10 condensed. The part of this course that matters longest.

## The standard

**You are accountable for what you send.** "The AI told me" is not a defence anyone accepts.

> If you would not put your name to a claim without checking it when a colleague told you, do not put your name to it when a model told you.

## Verify these, always

- **Citations** -- every one. Not a sample.
- **Numbers** -- statistics, dates, prices, measurements
- **Names and details about real people**
- **Anything after the knowledge cutoff**
- **Anything asserting how something works**

## Where hallucination is worst and least

**Worst:** citations, specific numbers, details about real people, niche technical detail, anything that does not exist.

**Least:** transformation of text you supplied -- summarising, rewriting, translating, extracting.

**Asking a model to recall is risky. Asking it to transform is much safer.** Structure your work around that.

## Two cheap wins

1. **Supply the source.** Paste the document rather than asking from memory.
2. **Permit uncertainty.** *"If you are not certain, say so. Do not guess."*

## One thing that does not work

**Asking the model whether it is sure.** There is no confidence signal inside for it to report. It will confidently affirm a fabrication.

## Never

- **Evaluate people** -- screening, ranking or scoring candidates or students
- **Decide whether someone did something wrong** -- cheating, fraud, misconduct
- **Create synthetic media of a real person** without explicit, informed consent
- **Create synthetic intimate imagery** of anyone
- **Clone a voice** without consent
- **Paste credentials** into any tool
- **Paste other people's personal data** without a basis

## Before pasting anything

- Is this mine, or does it contain information about someone else?
- Would they mind?
- Do I actually need the identifying detail for the help I want?
- Does my organisation permit this tool for this data?
- Is my input used for training? *(Check the setting. The default is often not what you assume.)*

## Protect yourself and your people

**Agree a code word** with family and close colleagues, for unexpected urgent requests. A cloned voice does not know it. Free, two minutes, and the single most effective defence available to an individual.

**Verify through another channel.** Call back on a known number -- not the one that called you.

**Be suspicious of urgency.** It exists to prevent verification.

## When not to use AI at all

Four tests. Any "yes" is a stop.

1. Would being confidently wrong cause **serious harm**?
2. Does it require **accountability** someone must own?
3. Is **being human** the point -- condolence, apology, a personal message?
4. Does the **data** forbid it?

Also: when you need to learn the thing; when checking costs more than doing; when it makes you less careful; when you could not defend the output.

**Not using it is not a failure state.** Ask a person. Look it up. Do it yourself. Use a calculator.

## Building something

**Prompt injection has no complete fix.** If your application feeds external content to a model, that content can carry instructions.

- Limit what any tool can reach; narrowest access that works
- Validate model output before acting on it
- **Keep a human confirming anything consequential** -- sending, paying, deleting, publishing
- Log everything

## Disclosure

Say so when a viewer would otherwise be misled. The test:

> Would they feel misled if they found out afterwards exactly how this was made?

Generated background music: no. A synthetic presenter taken for a real person: yes. Generated footage presented as a record of something that happened: definitely.

## Verification that survives a real week

Make it a **step, not an intention**. On the checklist, in the template, at the moment something becomes shared.

**Mark every claim first, then verify as a batch.** Faster than interleaving, and you see the total.

Where you could not check something, **say so in one sentence**. That transfers the risk honestly instead of hiding it.
